title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 118: The Ancient Stepwells of Western India
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 118 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Ancient Stepwells of Western India

Paragraph 1. In dry parts of western India, ancient people built amazing stone water places called stepwells. In regular wells, people stand at the top and pull water up with ropes and buckets. However, a stepwell is very different. It is a deep stone hole in the ground with long stairs going down to the water.

Paragraph 2. People built these wells because of the local weather. For nine months each year, the weather is very hot and dry. Then heavy rains fall for only a few weeks. Because sandy soil drinks rainwater fast, ancient builders dug deep down to reach underground water areas called aquifers. During dry summer months, the water dropped low, so villagers walked down hundreds of stone steps to collect water.

Paragraph 3. Between 600 and 1600 CE, stepwells became beautiful stone buildings. Kings, rich traders, and royal women paid for them. The most famous one is Rani ki Vav in Gujarat. A queen ordered it in 1063 to remember her dead husband. Workers carved hundreds of stone pictures of gods and dancers on its walls. Stepwells were also important social places where village women met every day to talk and share news. The deep stone walls kept the bottom six to ten degrees cooler than the hot air outside.

Paragraph 4. In the 1800s, British rulers thought stepwells were dirty because people stepped directly into the water with their feet and pots. This spread dangerous stomach sicknesses. Therefore, British rulers built metal water pumps and closed many old wells with bricks. Today, India lacks underground water again, so workers are cleaning old stepwells to save rainwater for modern towns.
